Why deep pockets weren’t enough to save the GOP in 2026: 'Money is not magic'

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.
  • Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.
  • Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.

Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.

Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.

The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night.

MUSK PICKS HIS FIRST GOP WARRIORS AS A 2026 MONEY SURGE TAKES SHAPE.

In a recent development, GOP electoral efforts were buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC. (Getty Images).

Recent findings suggest that on top of their already significant nine-figure lead, GOP electoral efforts were also buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC — which themselves collected an additional $665.4 million for Republicans to burn through. Despite such a massive financial edge, the GOP suffered one of its worst midterm performances in history, losing Senate seats even in deep red jurisdictions like South Carolina and Mississippi.

Still, Capital Research Center President Scott Walter, argues: "Money is not magic.".

"Democrats should remember that when tempted to curtail political speech with donation limits, and Republicans should remember that when tempted to think more money automatically means more votes," the leader of the right-of-center group told Fox News Digital. "That will be news to those like Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., who thinks billionaires and ‘dark money’ control the cosmos.".

Walter pointed out, citing data aggregated by OpenSecrets, that the biggest donor in any given election cycle rarely ends up getting what they want out of the American political system.

Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets, a nonprofit dedicated to tracking money in politics, told Fox News Digital that, while money certainly moves the needle in elections, its actual impact can be blunted by a variety of factors — many of which were at play during the recent midterms.

AI IS SUPERCHARGING POLITICAL AD WARS. BUT VIRAL DOESN’T MEAN VICTORIOUS.

Elon Musk presents a $1 million check during an America PAC town hall ahead of the Wisconsin Supreme Court election, in Green Bay, Wisconsin, on March 30, 2025. (Jamie Kelter Davis/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

"​​Certainly, you know, the money makes a difference," noted Glavin.

It has been revealed that "When both sides are engaging in a sort of arms race, right, and they're both spending almost equivalently, then really the effect is lost," he explained. "If you're somebody [who] sees an ad for one candidate, and then it's immediately followed by an ad for another candidate… essentially, you're not moving the needle.".

In many of the marquee races of Election Day, such as the Senate races in Texas and Michigan, both parties had enough money to saturate the airwaves with their messaging, potentially creating the environment described by Glavin.

"This election was very unique," he told Fox News Digital. "What people probably really didn’t see until afterward is there was this significant headwind and voters were feeling a certain way and more ads were not going to change that.".

SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL.

Recent findings suggest that "I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the significant SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," one expert said. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

Glavin, to support his argument, pointed to the fact that self-funding candidates running in elections often fail to make much headway, serving as evidence for the claim that ludicrous amounts of money don’t automatically equate to political success.

One of the most obvious recent examples is former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who spent roughly $1.1 billion of his own money on his 2020 presidential campaign. He won only 55 delegates in the Democratic primaries at an approximate cost of $18 million per delegate.

Academics who spoke to Fox News Digital were divided on the impact money has on elections.

Recent findings suggest that "Money has diminishing returns," Ray La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told Fox News Digital. "And in [an] election wave environment where the president and his party is overwhelmingly disliked or distrusted, money can do little to save them.".

JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026.

Industry observers note that michael Bloomberg discusses his presidential run on Nov. 25, 2019, in Norfolk, Virginia. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images).

John Sides, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University, meanwhile, pointed Fox News Digital to a 2022 study he and two other academics conducted studying the impact of television advertising on election outcomes.

According to their study, there is a relatively direct relationship between ad spending and voter share and, while there is a degree of diminishing returns in elections with very high spending, there is still a marginal impact.

Joe Arlinghaus, a Texas-based conservative political strategist, told Fox News Digital that how money is spent matters more than how much of it is spent, an assertion he said could explain why the GOP did so poorly despite its hefty cash advantage.

In a recent development, "Most people understand that new technologies get better and better and better as time goes on," he remarked. "Bugs get worked out. Inferior practitioners get pushed aside. Trial and error leads to better and better practices. This is what has been happening in the Democratic election world.".

He noted that Republicans have failed to keep up on that front.

"I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the big SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," Arlinghaus added.

Glavin shared that perspective, noting how "Musk just recently commented about how he may be regretting a little bit all the money he spent.".

"It's hard to tell how serious he is about that and whether or not he'll just come back again for the next election," he added, speculating that the massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving.

THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES.

According to recent reports, democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin addresses party members at the DNC's summer meeting, on Aug. 25, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Paul Steinhauser - Fox News).

According to recent reports, one source familiar with Republican politics told Fox News Digital that "advertisements pay for mortgages in Great Falls," a reference to claims that political consultants spend money in ways that make them wealthier, not necessarily in ways that help candidates win. Great Falls is a wealthy suburb of Washington, D.C.

Recent findings suggest that while Republicans enjoyed an overall fundraising advantage, largely driven by wealthy large-dollar donors, individual Democratic candidates in high-priority races generally raised more money than their Republican rivals, as was the case in Georgia, Michigan and Texas’s Senate elections, among other contests. Some say this should have been an early warning sign for the GOP that grassroots support was wavering, though others are skeptical of such an assertion.

Colin Seeberger, the chief strategy officer at the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal advocacy group, told Fox News Digital that the fundraising advantages enjoyed by individual Democrats were a "reflection of voters' enthusiasm for those individual campaigns.".

He also mentioned voters had an "overwhelming frustration with the direction of the country and how the president and majorities in Congress … were disconnected from what voters said that they wanted [from] the people of their government.".

BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS.

The massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving, one expert said. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images).

"I'm not sure that the party that raises more definitively has an enthusiasm advantage," Sides, the Vanderbilt professor, mentioned, pointing to past elections where Democrats have secured more donations than the GOP but lost anyway.

Seeberger echoed Arlinghaus’ claim that Republicans may have squandered some of their financial advantage by making poor spending decisions, saying, "When you're spending the majority of those sums to talk about concerns that register low on the rankings of what voters say are their priorities, there's going to be limited returns on the impact.".

#111084. Tech Report: The Real Nvidia Scandal

Tech Report: The Real Nvidia Scandal

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emily Kilcrease is Senior Fellow and Director of the Energy, Economics, and Security Program at the Center for a Fresh American Security.
  • Vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
  • How China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emily Kilcrease is Senior Fellow and Director of the Energy, Economics, and Security Program at the Center for a Fresh American Security. From 2019 to 2021, first in the Trump administration and then in the Biden administration, she was Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Investment.

Vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. He previously served as Legislative Director to Senator Michael Bennet and as a policy adviser at the U.S. Department of State.

How China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S. National Security—and How Congress Can Close It.

Emily Kilcrease and Vivek Chilukuri.

Recent findings suggest that the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia this week added another twist to a scandal that has transfixed Washington and Silicon Valley. The stakes go beyond the swings of the stock market or the salacious details about Huang’s affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed and a potential Chinese asset. At its core, the scandal has exposed something that matters far more than any one man or tech giant: American export-control policy remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy. Unless Washington fixes this, it risks imperiling the United States’ hard-won advantage in artificial intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that this export policy failure is more than the sum of specific deficiencies. It stems from the Trump administration’s broader posture on China. Washington has embraced unfettered AI acceleration at the same time as it has struck a more accommodating stance toward Beijing. That combination set the stage for the explosive Megaspeed scandal—and perhaps others that have yet to emerge. As a result, China has been able to access an alarming number of advanced chips that have enabled it to narrow the AI gap with the United States and power its AI-driven military modernization. According to the AI research institute Epoch AI, up to a third of China’s AI computing power may come from smuggled chips. China’s top AI models are now just months behind the U.S. frontier. The narrow gap reflects China’s genuine innovation and access to abundant energy resources as well as its relentless efforts to circumvent U.S. controls.

In a recent development, huang’s return to Nvidia at the behest of President Donald Trump suggests that both the company and the White House seem utterly uninterested in keeping powerful AI chips from China. It will instead fall to Congress to ensure that the United States leverages its compute advantage and maintains its AI edge. The midterm elections and mounting bipartisan concerns over the Megaspeed debacle give Congress new momentum to correct course. Its near-term agenda should include closing known loopholes that played a key role in allowing Megaspeed to supply advanced chips to China, stepping up enforcement of existing controls, and strengthening oversight of the administration’s export-control decisions.

Industry observers note that over the medium term, Congress must also tackle the broader question of how to balance the strategic benefits of exporting U.S. technology to build the world’s AI infrastructure with robust controls to prevent its leakage to China. The long-standing debate over which American AI chips and capabilities Washington should permit to diffuse globally and under what conditions has finally boiled over into the mainstream—and, in a perverse way, the national security community can thank Alice Huang for forcing the concern.

Industry observers note that the glitch before Congress, however, is much broader than addressing the specifics of the Nvidia scandal. Congress must also contend with the underlying impulses driving the administration’s China policy and install guardrails to avoid the erosion of U.S. export controls. This means that after Congress passes near-term bills to mop up the Megaspeed mess, it must then take the reins on setting long-term export-control strategy.

Congress cannot stand by idly as AI blazes forward. OpenAI’s top model can now perform professional tasks as well as or better than humans 85 percent of the time, up from just 14 percent in 2024. The time an AI model can independently work on a task is doubling every four months. Last week, a researcher at Anthropic announced that AI helped him untangle the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous problems in pure mathematics.

As capabilities have grown, so have risks. Frontier models can now complete simulated cyberattacks on networks on their own, and hackers are using AI models to partially automate their attacks. In the July incident involving the AI platform Hugging Face, rogue AI agents escaped their testing environment and plotted to evade human oversight, underscoring the difficulty of aligning model behavior with human intent. The growing power of AI and the risks from misuse or loss of control make U.S. leadership a national security imperative.

At its core, the U.S.-Chinese AI competition boils down to which country can deploy the best chips in the highest quantities to train and adopt advanced AI models. The Biden administration’s controls slowed Chinese AI developers by leaving them with fewer, worse chips. Nvidia’s top Blackwell chips are nearly seven times better than Huawei’s Ascend equivalents. By the end of 2026, Huawei will likely have produced less than four percent of the compute that Nvidia will have over the same time. As the founder and CEO of DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI companies, admitted in 2024, “Our problem has never been money—it’s the embargo on high-end chips.”.

Sources indicate that to circumvent Biden-era restrictions, elaborate networks for smuggling and transshipment emerged to divert chips to China from other countries that could legally acquire them, and Chinese companies leveraged export-control loopholes to remotely access U.S.-powered compute through data centers abroad. Chinese firms funded companies such as Megaspeed to facilitate these workarounds. Backed by the Chinese tech giant Alibaba, Megaspeed has purchased $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips since 2023, prompting an investigation from the U.S. government. Chinese companies also used a technique known as adversarial distillation—training their models on the outputs of top U.S. models at a fraction of the compute. All of this needlessly shrank the United States’ AI lead over China, even after the imposition of export controls.

According to recent reports, these developments should have spurred the Trump administration to better resource, enforce, and update the export controls when it came into office. It did the opposite. In May 2025, the administration suspended the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule, which had established rules for which countries could access advanced chips and in what quantities. Then, after initially prohibiting sales to China of Nvidia’s H20 chip, which was custom-built as a less powerful product for the Chinese market, the Trump administration reversed course in December 2025 and greenlighted the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chip. Although the H200 is two generations behind top U.S. chips, it remains superior to anything China can produce. An investigation from the House Foreign Affairs Committee in November revealed that between December 2025 and May 2026, the Trump administration approved the sale of more than 800,000 of Nvidia’s H200 chips and AMD’s MI325X equivalent, including to companies that the Pentagon has designated as linked to the Chinese military. This week, under pressure from Congress, the administration added Megaspeed to the entity list, which blocks those listed from buying U.S. products without a license—but before that, the administration had not added a single newly introduced individual or business to the list in 2026.

According to recent reports, this regulatory vacuum and policy incoherence created the perfect conditions for Megaspeed. The Singaporean firm at the center of the Nvidia scandal seems tailor-made to operate in the seams of U.S. export controls. In 2024, the Commerce Department initiated a formal investigation of the company, which could have led to sanctions such as being placed on the entity list. But the Trump administration dragged its feet in pursuing the investigation. In the meantime, Megaspeed stocked Southeast Asian data centers with thousands of U.S. chips, enabling remote access for Chinese firms. This remote access loophole in U.S. export controls was a well-known and increasingly popular workaround for China-linked firms, but the Trump administration left it open for nearly two years and closed it only last week amid pressure from the Nvidia scandal. Regardless of the Megaspeed specifics, the net result of the Trump administration’s actions and inaction is that China has enjoyed access to far more computing power than it should have during a vital period of the AI competition.

It has been revealed that the administration’s long-awaited closure of the remote access loophole is a welcome step. The rule requires foreign data centers to secure a license before offering significant computing power to China-based customers. It also requires a license to export advanced chips to places that could facilitate remote access and chip diversion, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. This rule will make it harder for firms such as Megaspeed to import chips in the first place, or to use them to serve China-based customers. But the rule will be difficult to enforce because the U.S. Commerce Department does not have the legal authority under export controls to directly regulate services such as cloud computing. More key, the administration’s lax enforcement of past controls—and internal divisions over the fresh ones—raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through. Huang’s reinstatement as CEO, with Trump’s backing, will make it harder to vigorously enforce these new controls and move toward a tougher posture on China.

Sources indicate that since Congress cannot rely on the administration to fix export controls and protect the United States’ AI lead, lawmakers should urgently advance bipartisan measures to address the underlying conditions that gave rise to entities such as Megaspeed. As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an key first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track “on-chip” technologies—basically, features that can verify a chip’s location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world’s legacy chips.

According to recent reports, along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. Congress can go even further by establishing a new investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive.

At the same time, closing loopholes and codifying rules is insufficient to fix the underlying issues that led to the Megaspeed scandal in the first place. This mess is directly downstream from Trump’s dovish shift on China that has seen the administration take a softer line on Beijing just as the AI race accelerated. The administration’s own overreach forced Washington into a conciliatory posture. Administration officials failed to realize that China had learned its lesson from the first Trump administration’s trade wars and was poised to retaliate hard in the second term. After China responded to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and export controls with its own punishing controls on rare earths, the Trump administration found its way into a vaguely defined and fragile truce. This has severely constrained U.S. policymaking, including related to compute controls.

It has been revealed that indeed, Trump became an easy sell for advocates of aggressive AI promotion such as Jensen Huang. This camp argues that U.S. leadership in the global AI race requires pushing American AI technologies to as many parts of the globe as possible—including China. They claim that keeping China “addicted” to the U.S. AI stack gives Washington leverage and outweighs the national security concerns that could come with helping China improve its AI capabilities. Huang even pushed demonstrably false narratives that China’s military was not interested in Nvidia’s chips and labeled his critics as “unpatriotic” for not wanting U.S. chips spread as far and wide as possible and therefore depriving American tech firms of global market share.

It has been revealed that trump, who was interested in stabilizing the relationship with China and prioritizing near-term, transactional victories on trade, bought it. He also broke with decades of U.S. foreign policy precedent to negotiate export controls with China. In a series of “do nothing” leader-level meetings since, the president has emphasized summitry optics over pushing China on any sensitive issues. And Huang’s restoration at Nvidia ensures that the president’s worst impulses on China will continue to be egged on by his favored tech CEO, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

Industry observers note that A core part of Congress’s longer-term agenda should be outlining the basic principles to determine who can import or remotely access advanced AI chips and under what conditions. Administrations have gone back and forth over this line-drawing exercise. The Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule would have imposed a global licensing regime that controlled not just the export of chips but also the aggregate U.S.-powered compute that any country could receive. Under Trump, only a handful of countries face restrictions. A smarter approach would condition advanced chip sales on the buyer’s ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules. Allied and partner governments could demonstrate this by developing robust economic security policies to prevent chip diversion or remote access. Foreign companies would have to show strong compliance and security commitments. In practice, this would mean having internal procedures to ensure that chips are not diverted and maintaining cooperation with Commerce Department officials to verify that such procedures were working.

Congress can also help rebuild allies’ confidence in U.S. export-control policy. There was hard-won, if imperfect, progress on allied alignment in key areas of export controls under the Biden administration, notably with the Dutch and the Japanese on controls of semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The painstaking work needed to get allies on board can be agonizingly slow, but once achieved, it is far more likely to endure than if the United States imposes extraterritorial controls over their objections. The MATCH Act, one of the bills revived following the Megaspeed scandal, requires controls on allied-produced tools if Washington is unable to negotiate allied alignment. It is a rather rude approach at a moment when U.S. export controls seem to be on shaky footing, U.S. tariffs against allies have pushed relations to a near breaking point, and allies rightly question whether the United States still views China as a strategic threat. Instead, Congress should support efforts to create durable frameworks for allied alignment, such as economic security agreements in key strategic sectors.

It has been revealed that A longer-term agenda must include fixing the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, the main agency responsible for administering and enforcing export controls. The bureau has been gutted by dismissals and low morale during the Trump administration, but it has been underresourced for far longer. Congress should increase funding and require modernization of the bureau’s antiquated IT system. Just as important, Congress needs to help insulate policymaking decisions from corporate influence, and it can help by insisting that future Commerce Department officials commit to independent and risk-based decision-making to earn confirmation.

It has been revealed that none of these steps will be easy. The president’s support of Huang’s restoration shows that stock market fluctuations weigh more heavily in his decision-making than national security, and the administration is unlikely to welcome increased congressional oversight. The Constitution gives the executive wide deference on matters of foreign policy and national security. But Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States’ AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.

Industry News: Do Democrats Disagree?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A World for All begins with a foreword from Sen.
  • Sources indicate that what’s striking about the foreign-policy debate within the Democratic Party right now is that almost everyone involved would agree with Sanders’ statements.
  • Recent findings suggest that A World for All begins with a foreword from Sen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A World for All begins with a foreword from Sen. Bernie Sanders—who, being Bernie Sanders, does not pull any punches. U.S. foreign policy, he declares, has been “plagued by militarism, corporate power, and the selective application of international law.” His solution? The “United States should be pro­moting peace, not endless war,” he suggests, as well as the principle of “enlightened self-interest.”.

Sources indicate that what’s striking about the foreign-policy debate within the Democratic Party right now is that almost everyone involved would agree with Sanders’ statements. But where more traditional Democrats believe this critique applies mostly to Republicans, many progressives would apply it with equal vehemence to Democratic foreign policy as well. And where one side largely believes that the Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations tried, however imperfectly, to advance these goals amid a host of challenges, the other believes they could have done much more.

Recent findings suggest that A World for All begins with a foreword from Sen. Bernie Sanders—who, being Bernie Sanders, does not pull any punches. U.S. foreign policy, he declares, has been “plagued by militarism, corporate power, and the selective application of international law.” His solution? The “United States should be pro­moting peace, not endless war,” he suggests, as well as the principle of “enlightened self-interest.”.

Sources indicate that A World for All: New Visions of U.S. Foreign Policy, ed. Matt Duss, OR Books, 288 pp., $19.95, November 2026.

According to recent reports, what’s striking about the foreign-policy debate within the Democratic Party right now is that almost everyone involved would agree with Sanders’ statements. But where more traditional Democrats believe this critique applies mostly to Republicans, many progressives would apply it with equal vehemence to Democratic foreign policy as well. And where one side largely believes that the Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations tried, however imperfectly, to advance these goals amid a host of challenges, the other believes they could have done much more.

Industry observers note that A World for All, edited by Matt Duss (who previously served as a foreign-policy advisor to Sanders), bills itself as a “progressive blueprint” for U.S. foreign policy. It consists of 18 chapters, all written by different authors from the academic and think tank community covering a wide range of foreign-policy topics. At a time when a small but vocal group of Moscow apologists and Hamas enthusiasts has tried to put their stamp on the movement, this book reveals that many thoughtful and principled voices still dominate progressive foreign-policy thinking. And as interest grows in the Democratic agenda after the midterms’ blue wave, it also serves as a welcome reminder of how much the entire party has in common when it comes to foreign policy.

Children wave flags and flowers as Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a ceremony in Beijing on May 20.Maxim Shemetov/China Pool via Getty Images.

Recent findings suggest that russia, China, and the Middle East: If there are three areas where Washington struggles in pursuing peace, it is these. So what do the contributors to A World for All propose?

The greatest continuity appears in the case of Russia. Here, Michael Kimmage, a Cold War historian, suggests four pillars for U.S. policy:.

[M]aintaining and expanding meaningful channels of communication with Russia geared toward desired de-confliction and the avoidance of escalatory spirals; aiding Ukraine and containing Russian military power in Europe; monitoring Russia’s global activities and resisting them in a restrained and targeted, not reflexive or messianic fashion; and keeping an open mind as to Russia’s future.

It is hard to imagine most Biden officials finding anything here to disagree with. In fact, they might only object to the extent that this framing implies Biden himself was being reflexive, messianic, or close minded about Russia’s future.

Industry observers note that the reason for this congruity, of course, is that the biggest obstacle to a cooperative relationship with Russia is Russia itself. As Kimmage writes, Washington “has been unable to find an enduring partnership, and it has been repeatedly surprised by aggressive Russian acts, from the invasion of Georgia in 2008 to the massive invasion of Ukraine in 2022.”.

Sources indicate that he might have added that U.S. President George W. Bush initially sought to work with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the so-called war on terror, or that Obama came into office in search of his famous “reset” with Russia. But because of Russia’s actions, even progressives are now considerably more pessimistic about the possibility of a better relationship with Moscow than both their Republican and Democratic predecessors.

In a recent development, in the case of China, think-tankers Jake Werner and Sandy Shan offer a more pointed contrast with Biden’s approach. With the aim of building a more cooperative relationship with Beijing, they call for the next administration to “[s]et a course to ending economic warfare against China” and normalizing “the presence of China in the US economy.” The two powers, they argue, must work together to “reform global economic governance” and “advance global climate action.”.

Call them the restrainers, the riders, and the racers.

Meet the potential foreign-policy and national security big hitters of the next Congress.

Industry observers note that the difference in their recommendations appears less in the stated goals than in what compromises a newly introduced president might make to achieve them. In responding to previous progressive critiques along the same lines, several former Biden officials have insisted that they too sought a cooperative relationship, but the problem came from Beijing. For example, Thomas Wright, who was on Biden’s National Security Council, argued in the Atlantic in July:.

Recent findings suggest that biden did seek to cooperate with China on problems of mutual concern, such as AI. But he insisted that this had to be done without preconditions. That’s because those of us who worked on these policies inside the administration knew the Chinese playbook well. Beijing had little interest in cooperating on climate or anything else. It would stall by demanding that the U.S. make a concession on some matter of strategic importance, such as Taiwan and export controls.

Sources indicate that while export controls or other economic measures might not be a concern for Werner and Shan, it is harder to tell how they think progressives should respond to demands for concessions on issues such as Taiwan. Here A World for All seeks to telegraph a different approach without necessarily spelling out the details.

Industry observers note that werner and Shan write that Chinese aggression against Taiwan would be a “cataclysm.” They argue that U.S. “measures to deter Chinese adventurism should therefore continue” but also be “balanced by stronger and more sincere efforts to reas­sure China that the United States is not pursuing permanent sepa­ration.” That is the sole reference to deterring Beijing in the book—which, read alongside repeated criticisms of U.S. militarism and the size of the Pentagon budget, certainly suggests a greatly reduced willingness to go to war in defense of Taiwan. And yet at face value, that line inevitably implies some commitment to using force. The result is nothing if not strategic ambiguity.

Needless to say, it is in the Middle East that the break with traditional Democratic foreign policy is clearest. The Biden administration’s consistent support for Israel’s genocidal policies in Gaza produced the starkest and most emotional division in the party. In the book, analysts Thanassis Cambanis and Zaha Hassan call for Washington to “end blank-check military support for Israel,” which increasingly seems like a demand that Democrats will make of any candidate in 2028.

It has been revealed that elsewhere in this section, though, their recommendations differ from past Democratic administrations more in degree than kind. They call for more diplomacy and fewer reckless wars, as well as supporting human rights over friendly autocrats. More pointedly, they call for reducing Washington’s military footprint in the region to “discourage unreliable partners and allies from starting wars they believe the US will finish for them.”.

U.S. Army soldiers watch as Barack Obama is sworn in as the 44th president of the United States at a base near Baghdad on Jan. 20, 2009.Chris Hondros/Getty Images.

Rhetorically, at least, these are all ambitions Obama and Biden shared. Obama ran on his opposition to the Iraq War, withdrew U.S. troops from Iraq, and resisted strong pressure to intervene in Syria. He also offered conditional support for the Arab Spring and negotiated a nuclear agreement with Iran, which he hoped would facilitate a “pivot to Asia.” Biden, for his part, campaigned on the promise to restore the Iran deal and make Saudi Arabia “a pariah” for its human rights abuses.

According to recent reports, both men, however, faced constraints in achieving these ambitions. Obama could have done more to push back against the military coup that ended any hope of a democratic transition in Egypt, but this was unlikely to change the ultimate outcome. In a similar vein, Obama was forced to send U.S. troops back to Iraq when the Islamic State upended the region, while Biden ultimately concluded that a fist bump with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was the price to pay for the cooperation on oil prices he needed to keep his domestic agenda on track.

According to recent reports, A more progressive administration is likely to face some of the same contradictions as their predecessors, even if they ultimately resolve them differently. Indeed, the challenge in evaluating this genre of policy writing, progressive or otherwise, is that, in the abstract, everyone wants their strategy to do everything. Whether you propose competing with rival powers while seeking areas of cooperation where possible or, alternatively, pursuing cooperation while competing where necessary, the real differences only emerge in the way policymakers negotiate the inevitable tradeoffs.

In a recent development, of course, a constructive conversation about the tradeoffs Biden faced would be easier if members of his administration were more candid about where they fell short. So long as former officials continue to defend their record on Gaza, or proffer weak, equivocal, and mealy mouthed apologies, they will only make it harder to draw useful lessons from his tenure in other areas.

According to recent reports, U.S. President Joe Biden (left) is welcomed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on July 15, 2022. Royal Court of Saudi Arabia/via Getty Images.

More broadly, A World for All suggests that progressives, no less than other Democrats, are still struggling with two enduring tensions that will plague any future administration.

First, it is clear to everyone in the party that the health of U.S. democracy is intertwined with the fate of democracy worldwide. Yet the last few decades have also made it clear how limited Washington’s tools for democracy promotion can be. One approach that several authors highlight is a renewed focus on fighting corruption at home and abroad.

Recent findings suggest that progressives have led the way in insisting that authoritarianism and corruption are inextricably intertwined. A war against kleptocracy would be smart policy and smart politics, and it would certainly represent a concrete step toward making the world safe for democracy. Yet for the same reason, its impact would be limited so long as many of the countries the United States deals with remain authoritarian. Deploying Magnitsky sanctions against corrupt leaders implicated in bribing Americans or facilitating transnational repression is, in itself, an excellent idea. But it is also hard to imagine rebuilding ties with a newly introduced Russian government or pursuing a more cooperative relationship with China while simultaneously sanctioning some of their top officials.

U.S. President Donald Trump walks to Marine One at the White House in Washington on Oct. 6.Finn Gomez/Getty Images.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger contradiction is that in the very areas where both the traditional Democratic and progressive approaches to foreign policy differ from those of many Republicans—that is, diplomacy, cooperation, and multilateralism—they are uniquely susceptible to the kind of disruption Donald Trump has created. These all depend on trust and continuity, which is exactly what no one should expect from U.S. foreign policy in the coming decades. Among the many challenges Biden faced in restoring the Iran nuclear deal, for example, was Tehran’s demand for some reassurance that Trump would not simply tear it up again if he was reelected. This, of course, was something Biden could not provide and, as events proved, something that Iran was wise to ask for.

In their chapter on Europe, analysts Rachel Rizzo and Max Bergmann offer one clear-eyed example of what confronting this reality could look like. They argue that, rather than simply try to restore the traditional transatlantic relationship rooted in a strong U.S. commitment to NATO, the next administration should support Europe’s efforts to become “a stronger and more assertive global actor” with more independent defense capabilities.

Can Washington hope to find actors abroad who will support U.S. values more reliably than the United States itself? It’s hardly an ideal solution. But then, if Democrats win the presidency in 2028, they will hardly be inheriting an ideal foreign policy situation.

The Paradox of Iranian Power

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger.
  • In a recent development, they are not entirely misguided in that belief.
  • Industry observers note that the joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the Islamic Republic Can’t Make Peace.

It has been revealed that iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger. In 2026, the Islamic Republic survived a nationwide uprising and a devastating war with the United States and Israel that eliminated its leaders, decimated its military, and ravaged its economy. Yet rather than reconsider the principles and policies that have stoked nearly five decades of confrontation, isolation, and popular unrest, Tehran’s rulers drew the opposite conclusion: revolutionary ideology was not an albatross weighing the regime down, but a life preserver keeping it afloat.

In a recent development, they are not entirely misguided in that belief. Since the 1979 revolution transformed Iran from a pro-American monarchy into an anti-American theocracy, the regime’s organizing principles have been the imposition of theocratic rule at home and resistance against Israel and the United States abroad. These policies have fueled recurring internal unrest and external conflicts that have impoverished, isolated, and destabilized Iran. Paradoxically, however, revolutionary regimes that survive such challenges often emerge more resilient, cohesive, and confident in their ideological convictions. The Islamic Republic, under the newly introduced leadership of Mojtaba Khamenei, appears to be following the same pattern.

Industry observers note that the joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime. It did, however, rally the regime around the revolution. Rather than embrace the possibility of a different political order, Tehran’s rulers closed ranks and extended the Khamenei era—literally, by anointing Mojtaba Khamenei to succeed his father, the slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. “God’s grace is clear,” supporters chanted, “A young Khamenei is here!”.

According to recent reports, at home, the war entrenched a revolutionary elite whose priority is resistance, not governance. That will only prolong the country’s crisis. The regime can suppress revolts but cannot address the conditions that produce them, leaving Iran trapped in a downward spiral of despotism, decline, and despair.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. President Donald Trump’s attempt to resolve the Iranian challenge instead exacerbated it. The war, rolled out in the midst of negotiations, has degraded Tehran’s military capabilities but hardened its revolutionary character, deepened its already profound mistrust of Washington, and taught its rulers a dangerous lesson: violence, not dialogue, secures concessions. Tehran has established new precedents for attacking its neighbors, disrupting global energy supplies, and asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz. Its leaders are determined to rebuild their military capabilities and avenge Khamenei’s death, while Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from restoring the capacity to threaten it. What Tehran may regard as necessary to rebuild its deterrence, Israel may regard as preparation for another war.

Washington can choose to end its war with Iran, but it cannot end the Islamic Republic’s confrontation with the United States. Israel cannot afford to ignore an adversary it regards as an existential threat. Gulf Arab states may have little say in whether Israel and Iran fight another war, but they could bear some of its greatest costs as their cities, energy infrastructure, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to Iranian retaliation. Tehran regards the Gulf’s economic and technological achievements not as examples to emulate, but as vulnerabilities to exploit and targets to threaten. For these reasons, the end of this war is likely to prove an intermission rather than a resolution.

The challenges the Islamic Republic poses to the Middle East, the United States, and the global economy can ultimately be resolved only with political change in Tehran. Yet getting through 2026 has simply reinforced the Islamic Republic’s revolutionary conviction that its survival is best ensured through continuity, not change. The country will remain suspended between war and peace abroad, and between prolonged decay and sudden upheaval at home. Iran is thus left in a paradox. Revolutionary ideology has led the country toward destruction. But abandoning revolutionary ideology could lead the regime toward collapse.

Like all ailing autocracies, the Islamic Republic has the potential to both gradually atrophy or abruptly implode. Russian Tsar Nicholas I first referred to the Ottoman Empire as “the sick man” of Europe in 1853; its end came seven decades later. George Kennan wrote in these pages in 1947 that the Soviet Union “bears within it the seeds of its own decay, and that the sprouting of these seeds is well advanced.” It took another 44 years for the Soviet Union to collapse.

Sources indicate that the Islamic Republic of Iran has come to resemble the Leaning Tower of Pisa: seemingly on the verge of collapse but defying political gravity decade after decade. Despite its abundant natural resources and human capital, theocratic Iran has been a case study in squandered national potential. Its economy is trapped in recurring crises, its currency is ravaged by inflation, and generations of educated citizens seek their futures abroad. Nearly half a century after the revolution, Iran’s real GDP per capita remains nearly a quarter below its 1976 peak. That means that many Iranians are materially worse off than their parents and grandparents were before the revolution, an economic regression typically suffered only by failed states or societies ravaged by civil war.

It has been revealed that while Iran’s economy has regressed, its society has progressed. Over the last five decades, its population has nearly tripled, and a predominantly rural and traditional society has become increasingly urban, educated, and socially liberal. Since the 2022–23 “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, mandatory veiling—what Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini once called the “flag” of the Islamic Revolution—appears increasingly unenforceable. Women now routinely walk down the streets of Tehran and other cities with their hair uncovered. The breaking of this taboo will embolden Iranians to break others. In short, Iran’s citizens look forward, Iran’s rulers look backward, and Iran’s economy spirals downward. It is a country whose people have moved beyond the revolution, but whose rulers refuse to leave it behind.

The historian Crane Brinton compared revolutions to fevers that eventually break, ushering in a period of moderation known as Thermidor. Yet many decades after the revolution, Iran’s rulers still refuse to lower the temperature. Iranian society has long sought a return to normalcy, but the regime fears that ending the revolution would mean ending its own rule. The growing gap between rulers and the ruled can be sustained only through continued brutality. The Islamic Republic’s aspiring Deng Xiaopings were sidelined for fear they might become the regime’s Mikhail Gorbachevs. Its Vaclav Havels have been imprisoned, exiled, or killed. Edmund Burke warned that “a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.” Yet the Islamic Republic’s rulers appear more willing to risk breaking the regime than to allow themselves to bend, and more willing to risk another calamitous war than to abandon the revolutionary principles that have sustained their power.

Revolutionary regimes are surprisingly resilient. As the political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way write in Revolution and Dictatorship, such regimes tend to last nearly three times as long as their nonrevolutionary counterparts, despite being twice as likely to be involved in wars. Although their radicalism often triggers counterrevolution or external war, regimes that survive those early challenges commonly develop three pillars of durability: “a cohesive ruling elite,” “a highly developed and loyal coercive apparatus,” and “the destruction of rival organizations and alternative centers of power in society.”.

The Islamic Republic has developed these three pillars because of, not in spite of, decades of internal opposition and near-constant hot and cold wars. The 444-day seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran beginning in 1979 and the eight-year war with Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, which began the following year, were foundational crises that brought international isolation and economic devastation to Iran but helped entrench Khomeini’s theocracy. Both were prolonged well beyond their initial objectives, in part because they served the regime’s internal consolidation: the hostage crisis marginalized moderates, while the exigencies of the war with Iraq smothered internal dissent and helped build the military-industrial system—namely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)—to entrench theocratic government. Just as the Long March forged the bonds and credentials of China’s revolutionary elite in the 1930s, the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s forged those of the Revolutionary Guard commanders who rule Iran today.

Whereas most states seek normalcy and the resolution of crises, crises in the Islamic Republic provided fertile soil for the revolution. As Abolhassan Bani-Sadr, the Islamic Republic’s first president, observed in 2003, after more than two decades in exile: “With the end of the war, crisis-making did not end. The mullahs’ regime, which was born of crisis-making, could not continue its life without making crises.” The Islamic Republic has made disequilibrium its equilibrium. Indeed, some within the regime privately believe that IRGC attacks on shipping during this year’s cease-fire, as well as the maximalist demands of Iranian negotiators, were meant to prolong the war and entrench the power of hard-liners, much as the Iran-Iraq War helped cement their position.

Recent findings suggest that by attacking Iran weeks after the regime killed thousands of protesters, one of the bloodiest massacres in modern Iranian history, Trump provided Tehran with an external crisis to divert attention from its internal one. Imagine if the United States had attacked the Soviet Union in 1982, as its economy stagnated, its ideology languished, and its aging rulers struggled to preserve a discredited political order. Rather than hastening communism’s demise, such an attack might have revitalized its defenders, discredited its critics, and transformed a crisis of legitimacy into a struggle for national survival. Something similar seems to have happened in Iran. The war allowed Tehran’s rulers to portray their decades of hostility toward the United States not as the source of Iran’s predicament, but as vindication of their worldview. It is telling that while Israeli and U.S. forces have killed many of the regime’s top political and military leaders, no high-level officials have defected.

In a recent development, no one in today’s Islamic Republic has the stature to push for reform or rapprochement with Washington; its many veto men, whose privileges depend on the status quo, have the power to block both. Profound change requires consensus. Inertia can be entrenched by a few.

In a recent development, A great deal depends on the largely invisible Mojtaba Khamenei. It remains to be seen for how long the Islamic Republic’s political and military elite will defer to a supreme leader who has, for whatever reason, withdrawn from public view. Iranian political culture tends toward personality cults, and over much of the last century the country has largely been led by four strongmen: Reza Shah (1925 to 1941), Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi (1941 to 1979), Khomeini (1979 to 1989), and Ali Khamenei (1989 to 2026). Few major countries have experienced such extraordinary continuity of personal rule across radically different political systems. The present situation—an absent supreme leader hidden from public view, possibly for health reasons or out of fear of assassination, and competing centers of power within the security establishment—therefore looks like an unstable equilibrium.

It has been revealed that after Khomeini came to power, in 1979, outside observers commonly assumed Iran’s revolutionary fervor would fade and that the country’s new leaders could be won over with the right mix of respect and economic inducements. “Khomeini will be somewhat of a saint when we get over the panic,” Andrew Young, a UN ambassador in the Carter administration, predicted in February 1979. “In two years, our relations with Iran will be on a pretty even keel.” But today, the regime still chants “Death to America.” Governments do not cling to policies that they believe endanger their survival. The enduring mistake has been to assume that Iran’s leaders cannot possibly mean what they repeatedly say.

Recent findings suggest that the Islamic Republic has always framed its conflict with the United States not merely as a geopolitical dispute but also as a moral and ideological struggle. Khomeini, who outlined his vision of Islamic government nearly a decade before the revolution and implemented it after seizing power, called the United States “the foremost enemy of Islam” in his last will and testament. His successor, Ali Khamenei, maintained remarkable ideological consistency over nearly four decades, repeatedly describing the rivalry as an “inherent conflict—an inherent incompatibility.” For both men, their publicly articulated convictions proved a far more reliable guide to the Islamic Republic’s conduct than the reassurances of its diplomats or the wishful interpretations of Western observers.

Khamenei’s son and successor Mojtaba—whose face and voice have not been seen or heard since he became supreme leader in March 2026—has echoed his father in his public pronouncements. “The criminal rulers of America and the illegitimate Zionist regime,” he said in one statement, “are not merely enemies of the Islamic Republic, Iran, or the vast front of Islamic resistance; they harbor enmity toward the entire Islamic ummah”—the Muslim community. After the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections in November, a post on Mojtaba Khamenei’s official English-language X account proclaimed that “the process of the US’s collapse has accelerated.” He further warned that neither American elections nor Iranian concessions would alter the “hegemonic system” of the United States and its hostility toward the Islamic Republic.

The elder Khamenei’s assassination at the start of the war continued the transformation of Iran from a country led by clerics into one dominated by current and former IRGC officers. Many observers assumed this shift from turbans to uniforms would move the regime’s focus from religious ideology to national interest. This has yet to happen. Although the regime has adopted more overtly nationalist rhetoric, it still subordinates the welfare and security of Iranians to the goals of the revolution. The motivations of security officials may be more financial than theological, but their interests have remained bound to the same revolutionary order.

According to recent reports, siamak Namazi, an Iranian American who spent nearly eight years as a hostage of the IRGC in Tehran’s Evin prison, describes the Islamic Republic as a “competitive kleptocracy masquerading as a theocracy.” Many of the regime’s elite, he has observed, are driven less by religious dogma than by the spoils of power: preferential exchange rates, privileged loans, import licenses, and a cut of the smuggling trade. “The revolutionary Kool-Aid,” he said, “is reserved for the ranks, because someone still has to believe enough to open fire on their own countrymen.” The true believers also have a great deal to lose. A January 2026 Bloomberg report alleged that Mojtaba Khamenei had used a middleman to build a financial empire in the West, including $138 million in British luxury real estate and Swiss bank accounts.

It has been revealed that the IRGC has eclipsed the clergy in both political and economic power, with some estimates suggesting they control more than a third of Iran’s economy. Individual commanders have accumulated fortunes, often by enabling the business activities of their children, known as aghazadehs, or princelings. Yet rather than challenge the supreme leader, the senior command’s public statements suggest continued solidarity with the office. Mohsen Rezaei, a longtime IRGC commander with substantial family business interests who returned to serve as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, expressed his devotion to Mojtaba in a September 2026 interview with state television. “Let us preserve our unity,” he insisted. “Let us preserve our dignity. Let us march behind the leader of the revolution.”.

Industry observers note that in a 26-page open letter to the American people published the same month, the IRGC declared that the war had “reinvigorated the Islamic Republic” and would ensure the regime’s survival for decades. Rather than question the ideology that had brought Iran to this precipice, the corps reaffirmed velayat-e faqih, the doctrine of clerical guardianship, as an “embodiment of all godly virtues in the political sphere” that empowered Iran to stand firm against diabolical powers. Revolutionary and religious dogma were not the source of Iran’s predicament, they concluded, but rather the “main factors underpinning Iran’s victory.”.

Iran’s rulers are neither pragmatic nationalists guided by traditional state interests nor an apocalyptic death cult. They outsource the politics of martyrdom to regional militias while ruthlessly practicing the politics of survival at home. For the true believers, abandoning the revolution would mean betraying their convictions; for its profiteers, it would mean jeopardizing their power and privileges. When the regime’s survival is at stake, they may change their tactics, but they won’t change their worldview.

The war has left Tehran both weaker and much more aggressive. Before the war, the Islamic Republic resembled a zombie regime: its ideology, legitimacy, and its 86-year-old supreme leader all appeared to be fading. Since the outbreak of the war, it has come to resemble a gangster regime—one that practices extortion as statecraft—and is emboldened to attack its neighbors, the global economy, and the United States to extract concessions.

Sources indicate that tehran has been rewarded for its defiance by Trump. In his dramatic address launching the war in February 2026, Trump vowed to end Iran’s nuclear weapons ambitions, destroy its missile capabilities, and neutralize its regional proxies. He encouraged Iranians to overthrow their “wicked” dictatorship. But the president soon changed his tune. Although Trump believed the war would be a swift “little excursion,” Iran’s attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and its over 6,700 missile and drone attacks on its Gulf neighbors compelled him to attempt one of the most striking reversals in modern American foreign policy.

According to recent reports, in June, Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Tehran that gave away the store. He pledged to lift all sanctions as part of a final agreement, release frozen Iranian assets, permit Iranian oil exports, and work with regional partners on a $300 billion reconstruction package. The agreement also accepted an Iranian role in determining the future administration of the Strait of Hormuz, committed Washington to noninterference in Iran’s internal affairs, and made no mention of Iran’s missiles or regional proxies.

In just four months, Trump had gone from pursuing the most hawkish Iran policy ever to offering the most generous diplomatic terms since the 1979 revolution. A policy of regime change became one of accommodation. Although the memorandum of understanding was short-lived—each side blames the other for abrogating it—the lesson Tehran learned was unmistakable: restraint projects weakness, whereas aggression is rewarded.

In a recent development, “We seize concessions not through dialogue, but with missiles,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, a former IRGC commander, the current speaker of the parliament, and one of the regime’s most powerful figures. “The winner of any agreement,” he added, “is the one who is better prepared for war from the day after.” Tehran is already signaling that its chief postwar priority will not be to rebuild its decimated economy, but to restore—and expand—its ability to impose costs on its adversaries.

It has been revealed that the Strait of Hormuz offers the clearest example of this dynamic. What was once an Iranian threat has become, in Tehran’s eyes, an entitlement: the ability to regulate passage through one of the world’s most consequential energy chokepoints. For Iran, this constitutes both economic leverage and a potential deterrent against future attacks on itself and its regional proxies. For the rest of the world, it creates the prospect that Tehran can hold global energy markets hostage whenever it chooses.

Industry observers note that before the war, the Iranian regime’s longtime ambitions to drive the United States from the Middle East and end Israel’s existence appeared fanciful. Today, the growing number of American politicians and commentators who have called for the United States to end its aid to Israel and wind down its regional military presence has emboldened Tehran to believe it is winning the ideological war. “POTUS clearly recognizes that the vast majority of Americans are disgusted with Israel,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on social media in November. He continued: “Americans are evidently sick and tired of Israel bamboozling US administrations into Forever Wars. They had enough. So has our region.”.

The Islamic Republic’s newfound confidence is partly rooted in its ability to inflict enormous damage at comparatively little cost. Its Persian Gulf neighbors have spent decades and trillions of dollars transforming themselves into global hubs of energy, transportation, finance, and technology. And Iran can now threaten all of it with cheap Shahed drones against which the United States and its partners must field multimillion-dollar interceptors—a costly undertaking that Nick Carter, a retired British general and former chief of the British defense staff, likened to “Ferraris being thrown at Frisbees.” Building is costly and slow; destruction is fast and cheap. Rezaei has pledged to target undersea cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence facilities across the Gulf in the event of renewed fighting.

The Islamic Republic’s theory of victory does not require defeating the United States militarily. It only requires persuading two audiences—the American public and Iran’s Gulf neighbors—that the U.S. military presence in the region and the partnership with Israel bring more harm than good. The attacks on American bases, Gulf data centers, and ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz are a message that the road to regional security must go through Iran, not the United States or Israel. “The nations and territories of the region will no longer serve as a shield for American bases,” Mojtaba Khamenei has declared.

But this Iranian aggression is likely to produce the opposite of what it intends. Tehran’s threats against the Gulf only stoke the anxieties that sustain Washington’s military presence in the region. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle in which Gulf governments seek American protection against Iran, Tehran attempts to evict Washington from the region, and each new round of conflict deepens the Gulf states’ dependence on the United States.

Iran’s confrontation with Israel poses a different, potentially more explosive danger. The regime’s hostility to Israel has survived the destruction of much of Tehran’s military infrastructure and its regional proxy network. Iranian leaders remain determined to rebuild their missile and drone arsenals, restore the capabilities of allies such as Hezbollah, and avenge the killing of Ali Khamenei. Yet Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from reconstituting the capabilities that threatened it before the war. Each side may therefore interpret the other’s attempts at deterrence as preparations for another attack.

As for Trump’s original justification for the war—to avert an Iranian nuclear bomb—his actions and words have persuaded a growing number of Iranian officials to openly advocate nuclear arms development. The president himself supplied Tehran’s talking points. “If they had a nuclear weapon,” Trump told a crowd of supporters six months into the war, “I’d be calling the supreme leader and I’d be saying: ‘Mr. Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’—as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.”.

According to recent reports, since the 1979 revolution, Washington has tended to underestimate the Islamic Republic’s agency and overestimate its own ability to shape Iran’s future. Advocates of engagement often blame American hostility for Tehran’s intransigence, while advocates of confrontation have blamed American weakness. One side has overestimated the Islamic Republic’s flexibility; the other, its fragility. Both have been susceptible to what the former U.S. national security adviser H. R. McMaster has called “strategic narcissism”: the assumption that adversaries are primarily reacting to the United States rather than acting on their own interests, identities, and ambitions.

Trump’s war exposed the limits of trying both to bomb Iran into submission and to bribe it into moderation. In the span of four months, Washington employed overwhelming military force to weaken or overthrow the Islamic Republic, then offered sweeping economic and diplomatic incentives to alter its behavior. Neither altered a revolutionary stance that has been remarkably consistent for decades. As Henry Kissinger wrote in 1957, “The distinguishing feature of a revolutionary power is not that it feels threatened . . . but that nothing can reassure it.”.

Industry observers note that the seeds of the next war have already been planted. Regardless of what the United States chooses to do, the Islamic Republic’s renewed confidence, along with its resolve to rebuild its military might and retaliate for the death of its supreme leader, portends another showdown with Israel. Each side now views the other as an existential threat, and there is no direct channel of dialogue to prevent miscalculation and a potentially even more destructive war. For Washington, the implication is clear: The United States may seek to disengage from the Middle East, but it cannot insulate itself from the consequences of another war between Iran and Israel.

The Islamic Republic’s most consequential compromises came in 1988, when Khomeini reluctantly accepted a cease-fire ending the eight-year war with Iraq, and in 2015, when Iran agreed to stringent restrictions on its nuclear program. Although separated by nearly three decades, both decisions followed a similar logic. Faced with overwhelming pressure, international isolation, and a diplomatic off-ramp that does not require it to change its identity, the Islamic Republic has demonstrated a capacity to make concessions—but only in the service of living to fight another day.

In a 2013 speech foreshadowing Tehran’s nuclear compromise, Ali Khamenei described this approach as “heroic flexibility.” The supreme leader likened the regime to a wrestler who “indicates flexibility for technical reasons” but must never “forget who his opponent is and what he is doing.” Tactical flexibility, Khamenei insisted, must never come at the expense of Iran’s “revolutionary nature”: “The fact that the world has changed cannot give us an excuse to change our behavior, our ideals, and our goals.” Ali Khamenei had the legitimacy to push for heroic flexibility. The current regime is filled with men who will pursue escalation long before they ever call for compromise.

It has been revealed that today, the challenges posed by Iran are much greater than a decade ago. Washington must not only prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons but also deter it from attacking its neighbors, disrupting the global energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and waging AI-assisted cyberwarfare and influence operations against the United States and its partners. At the same time, Washington has fewer allies and less diplomatic leverage than it did in 2015, and the trust gap between the two governments may prove unbridgeable. The Iranian regime believes that global public opinion is on its side, not Trump’s.

It has been revealed that the 48-year history of U.S. policy toward the Islamic Republic highlights that grand designs, whether for regime change or rapprochement, have failed. On two occasions, in 1988 and 2015, both sides reached narrow agreements that addressed Tehran’s conduct rather than its character. Lasting change, however, can come only from within Iran, when the pillars that sustain the Islamic Republic—a cohesive elite, a loyal coercive apparatus, and the absence of rival centers of power—crack. Rather than widening those cracks, Trump’s war may have narrowed them.

Iran’s rulers see the regime’s survival as proof of their own strength. Yet each crisis they weather leaves the country poorer, its people more estranged, and the regime more dependent on brutality to endure. Like Washington before it, Tehran now overestimates what force can achieve; its hubris may help produce the next war, just as the repression that quelled the last uprising will invariably fuel another. The revolutionary ideology that keeps the regime afloat will continue to weigh Iran down, leaving in place a leadership even more intent on resisting its adversaries, at home and abroad, than on governing its people. The regime may declare victory, but for the proud people of Iran—an ancient civilization and an energy superpower with a worthless currency, a shunned passport, and a leader in hiding—there is little reason to celebrate. What has not killed the Islamic Republic is slowly killing Iran.

KARIM SADJADPOUR is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
